3.text: temporary trading-relations, and even with an individual belonging to a dif-

4.text: ferent people, — a Tungus or a Russian. The Chukchee call such trade-

5.text: acquaintances ɪnnaˊlêk (“friends”). Above I mentioned a case of group-mar-

6.text: riage with a Tungus. Wherever the Chukchee and the Tungus live in one

7.text: locality, numerous families of one of these peoples are united by group-

8.text: marriages to those of the other. A deviation from the common regulations

9.text: may be seen in the fact that the Chukchee have marital rights to the greater

10.text: part of married Tungus women; while, of the Tungus, only the most skilful

11.text: hunters, or those most friendly with the Chukchee, have similar rights to

12.text: Chukchee women. Many Russian families stand in similar relations of group-

13.text: marriage with the Chukchee; but the Chukchee are the only ones who look

14.text: upon these relations as upon group-marriage. The Russians, on the other

15.text: hand, are prone to see in them nothing but the loose conduct of women

16.text: anxious to receive payment in slaughtered reindeer. I should add, however,

17.text: that in some of the tales referring to ancient times, group-marriages with stran-

18.text: gers are also described; namely, with the Eskimo inhabitants of the opposite

19.text: American shore. The Chukchee, since ancient times, have cultivated trade-

20.text: relations with those people, such relations sometimes leading to those of group-

21.text: marriage. Even to-day, when the Eskimo traders from the American shore

22.text: arrive at the maritime Asiatic villages of the Chukchee and Eskimo, they

23.text: find temporary wives there in the houses of their friends. Similarly the

24.text: Chukchee traders have their temporary wives on the American shore.

28.text: Then a description of a contest between the two shamans is given. Kukuˊlpɪn

29.text: vanquished the shaman from Teˊpqän. “Says that shaman, ‘Let us at least

30.text: be companions in wives.’ — ‘Agreed!’ — ‘Where shall we go first? To

31.text: you? Where is your house?’ — ‘In the village Teˊpqän.’ — ‘How long does

32.text: it take you to fly there?’ — ‘About half a day.’ — ‘Aha! my house is nearer;

33.text: better let us go there. My two wives are at home. Let us race. The one

34.text: who arrives first shall sleep with both.’” Kukuˊlpɪn is again the winner,

35.text: arriving before his rival. After supper the latter is allowed to sleep with the

36.text: older wife, Kukuˊlpɪn himself sleeping with the younger one. The visitor is

37.text: dissatisfied with the arrangement, but submits after several fruitless attempts

38.text: to exchange sleeping-rooms with the host. Then both shamans fly to the

39.text: interior of the American Continent and carry away a young girl, the daughter

40.text: of an American chief. They bring her to the tent of Kukuˊlpɪn. Kukuˊlpɪn
